claims.text: The studied material is a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate.
The baseline coating has a coarse-grained microstructure and relatively low grain-boundary density.
Controlled annealing followed by rapid quenching will refine the FeNiCrCoCu coating's grain size relative to the as-deposited baseline.
The proposed grain refinement will increase grain-boundary density.
Oxidation and thermally activated diffusion are significant during sliding at 600–800 °C.
Increased grain-boundary density provides preferential sites for oxide formation or nucleation.
Increased grain-boundary density provides anchoring sites that improve oxide-scale adhesion.
A refined microstructure causes earlier onset of a protective oxide scale during high-temperature sliding.
A refined microstructure produces a more continuous protective oxide scale.
The protective oxide scale reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
The protective oxide scale lowers friction during sliding.
The refined-grained coating will have a lower wear rate than the coarse-grained baseline under identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
The refined-grained coating will exhibit reduced local strain localization.
The refined-grained coating will exhibit altered grain-boundary-sliding behavior.
The proposed mechanism should apply primarily at 600–800 °C and may weaken at lower temperatures.
Substrate interactions can dominate the coating's wear behavior and thereby limit the hypothesis.
Prior evidence in a similar high-entropy alloy links ultrafine grains and abundant grain boundaries to improved high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The magnitude of wear reduction and the specific microscopic-deformation changes have not been quantified.
